title: Why This Isn't the Dot-Com Bubble | Martin Casado on WSJ's BOLD NAMES

reader_summary.headline: Martin Casado explains why today's AI boom differs from the 1990s dot-com bubble.
reader_summary.overview: Martin Casado argues that current AI companies have strong cash reserves unlike the debt-ridden firms of the past. He notes that while the culture feels similar to the late 1990s, the financial situation is fundamentally different. Most investment now goes into physical infrastructure like data centers and power systems.

key_points.text: The 1990s crash involved fraud and debt, but today's AI firms have huge cash reserves and strong balance sheets.
key_points.evidence_quote: The dogcom crash wasn't just overvalued stocks. It was a fiber glut-financed by WorldCom, a company with 40 billion in debt that was cooking its books, compounded by 9-11.

key_points.text: Past tech bubbles started with silly ideas that later became huge successes, like a webcam coffee pot leading to Netflix.
key_points.evidence_quote: The first live video stream on the internet was a coffee pot. In 1991, a Cambridge researcher pointed a camera at the break room pot so he'd know whether there was coffee before walking downstairs.

key_points.text: High spending on AI infrastructure does not mean the economy will collapse because past overvaluations in mobile and cloud did not cause systemic failures.
key_points.evidence_quote: Remember, we overvalued things in, you know, mobile, we overvalued things during the early club. All of these things we overvalued. That did not result in systemic collapse.

notes: Christopher Mims and Tim Higgins of the Wall Street Journal sit down with a16z General Partner Martin Casado on WSJ’s Bold Names to ask whether the AI spending boom is a bubble waiting to burst. Martin explains why the fundamentals differ dramatically from the dot-com era—when WorldCom had $40 billion in debt versus today's tech giants with hundreds of billions on their balance sheets—and why a speculative valuation correction shouldn't be confused with systemic collapse. They also discuss where a16z sees opportunity in the "long tail" of AI companies beyond the state-of-the-art large language models. thesis: The speakers argue that the current influx of hundreds of billions of dollars into AI infrastructure resembles the mobile or cloud booms rather than the dot-com bubble, noting that the dot-com crash was driven by specific factors like a fiber glut, WorldCom's debt and accounting fraud, and 9-11, which are not present today. They suggest that while the current environment feels like a cultural and capital-fueled movement similar to the late 1990s, comparing valuations alone does not predict a systemic collapse.
